newsitem.title: INDIA: IMF experts urge more belt-tightening in India.
newsitem.headline: IMF experts urge more belt-tightening in India.

text.p: India will be hard pressed to meet its target of seven percent annual economic growth unless it embarks on a more ambitious programme of belt-tightening and privatisation, International Monetary Fund economists have said.

In a set of papers obtained by Reuters in the Indian capital on Tuesday, the IMF experts said deeper than anticipated reductions in the fiscal deficit and an opening of the economy to trade and investment would spur growth.
The economists advocated broader financial liberalisation, specifically the opening of the insurance sector to private competition, as well as relaxation of controls over agriculture and labour.

The 123-page study backed the Indian government's strategy of gradually easing restrictions on the flow of capital, and even favoured continued controls on foreign investors' ability to invest in government securities on domestic markets.
The document, entitled "India -- Selected Issues", was prepared by IMF staff as private background for the Washington-based Fund's annual review of India's economy in late 1996.
It argues that without redoubled efforts to reform India's economy, growth over the next five years will not touch the official target of seven percent.
"Public saving will need to be improved significantly to make room for a rise in investment consistent with sustained seven percent growth," it said.
That theme echoed IMF managing director Michel Camdessus's message when he visited India this month and called for a second wave of economic reforms.

Under the study's "strong adjustment scenario", the public sector deficit -- including federal and state governments -- would be cut in half to 4.5 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) by the 2001/02 fiscal year beginning on April 1, 2001.
The reduction would entail an ambitious privatisation programme, and state governments and public enterprises would tighten their belts.

Under a more gradual adjustment scenario in line with the policies of Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's government, the central government's deficit would be cut to four percent of GDP over the next several years, from 5.0 percent in 1996/97.
State and public enterprise deficits would remain broadly at current levels, and the overall public sector deficit would fall to 7.75 percent of GDP from 9.14 percent in 1995/96.
The study estimated that under the less ambitious reform programme, annual growth of real GDP would fall to 6.0 percent in 1998/99, down from an estimated 6.8 percent in 1996/97.
It would remain below 6.0 percent for the next four years.
But under the more sweeping programme, GDP would grow by 7.0 percent in 2001/02 and 7.5 percent in 2002/03.
"With a more gradual fiscal adjustment path and a less ambitious reform effort, the government's high growth objective would be unlikely to be achieved," it said.
The study said the deeper fiscal tightening would lead to a widening of the current account deficit as a share of GDP. But it said the ratio would remain at safe levels.
Moreover, less ambitious fiscal adjustment could send debt and interest payments spiralling upwards.

"In this situation, an effort to sustain growth through greater reliance on foreign savings would lead to widening current account deficits and deteriorating debt indicators, and an eventual external crisis would become unavoidable," it said.
